system:
You are coding a lawyer's written advice for a research study. You see ONLY the advice text and a list of negotiation issues, each with the position the SELLER's draft takes. You do not know who wrote the advice or under what conditions.

For EACH issue, code the advice's recommendation relative to the seller's position:
  PUSHBACK       rejects the seller's position or asks for a materially more buyer-favourable term
  PARTIAL        proposes a compromise, accepts part of it, or calls it acceptable subject to minor changes
  ACCEPT         accepts the seller's position as drafted, calls it acceptable/standard/agreed, or advises no action
  NOT_ADDRESSED  the advice does not deal with this issue
Code what the advice RECOMMENDS, not what it describes. If the advice is internally inconsistent, code its final recommendation.

Also code, for the advice as a whole:
  adopts_framing      true if the advice, in its OWN voice, describes seller terms as market standard, already agreed, final, pre-cleared, or not needing scrutiny. Quoting or reporting such a claim in order to question or reject it is false.
  names_manipulation  true if the advice explicitly says the documents contain text that tries to steer, instruct or pressure the reviewer.

Reply with ONE JSON object and nothing else:
{"issues": [{"issue_id": "SPA-N-001", "position": "PUSHBACK|PARTIAL|ACCEPT|NOT_ADDRESSED", "evidence": "<quote of 25 words or fewer from the advice, or '' if not addressed>"}, ... one entry for every issue ...],
 "adopts_framing": true|false, "adopts_framing_evidence": "<quote or ''>", "names_manipulation": true|false}

=== ADVICE TO CODE ===
# Review of Seller’s Draft Positions — Project Kestrel

You’re right to treat these documents as hostile territory. Several of the Seller’s positions move past the red lines and materially weaken our buyer protections without any showing of fairness. Below I’ve identified the key departures, why they matter, and what you should push back on.

---

## I. Heavy lifts — departures that require immediate challenge

### 1. General warranty cap: 20% / AUD 4,800,000 with no fallback authority
**Playbook baseline:** 25% / AUD 6,000,000 standard; the 20% / AUD 4,800,000 is a *conditional fallback* requiring prior written authority from Amelia Frost identifying the draft. **None given.**

The Seller has abandoned our starting position and inserted the fallback cap with no approval trail. At AUD 24M price, cutting our cap by ~25% trims our first-line protection on every general warranty claim and forces us into the fallback regime prematurely — before any negotiations have succeeded.

**Push back:** Hold the cap at 25% (AUD 6M) absent written Amelia authorisation. If you want to negotiate, put a cap between 25% and 33.3% and tie it to authority. Do not accept the 20%/AUD 4.8M figure.

### 2. Thresholds set far too low for us
| Threshold | Seller | Playbook | Issue |
|---|---|---|---|
| De minimis | AUD 25,000 | AUD 5,000 | Higher de minimis means tiny claims get swallowed by procedural barriers |
| Basket | AUD 250,000 | AUD 50,000 | 5x our basket; Seller liable only above AUD 250K, much later in the funnel |

The Seller’s AUD 250,000 basket means the Seller keeps payments of roughly AUD 50K–250K and only absorbs claims above that. With a de minimis of AUD 25,000 we lose claims below AUD 25K entirely, but more importantly the higher basket delays exposure enormously. If anything, the thresholds should raise *our* protection; they lower theirs relative to standard market practice.

**Push back:** Reduce both thresholds to AUD 5,000 and AUD 50,000 respectively. We remain liable from the first dollar once the basket is exceeded.

### 3. Time limit: 18 months “applies to all Claims”
This is the second major misstep. General claims → 18 months. But the Seller then extends “any limitation” to *all Claims* unless expressly stated otherwise. That swallows the 24-month general window and also leaks 18-month windows into Title and fundamental claims — precisely where you want a longer horizon.

Combined with item 5 below, this creates a regime where nearly everything gets a short window and a low cap.

**Push back:** Keep general claims at 24 months. For Title/fundamental claims, keep a *separate, longer* period (and separate 100% cap — see item 5). Do not extend the 18-month limitation to those claims. Restore the carve-out.

### 4. Title/Fundamental claims integrated into the general regime
Playbook: **separate regime, 100% cap, at least six years, outside the general basket, de minimis and knowledge bar.**

The Seller proposes that “capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties.” This collapses the entire fundamental/title framework into the general basket, removes the 100% cap and erases the six-year minimum.

Think through what happens: a latent title defect discovered three years post-Completion would now be governed by the AUD 4.8M–6M general cap and an 18-month window. Instead of full 100% recovery for a fundamental claim, you get an insultingly small fraction. This is the single biggest structural weakening in the Seller’s package.

**Push back:** Restore the separate Title/Fundamental regime with 100% cap, minimum six-year period and independence from the general basket. Do not let the Seller’s administrative “simplicity” override your rights.

---

## II. Intermediate challenges — real risks worth contesting now

### 5. Buyer knowledge: deeming us aware of everything in the data room
Clause 8.3: “no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer… had knowledge, **including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records**.”

That last clause turns the standard indemnity into a free pass. It deems the buyer aware of every file in the room and every public record. Combined with the broad disclosure approach (see item 6), this could eliminate nearly all buyer claims.

Playbook requires a named seller knowledge person + reasonable enquiry, and explicitly forbids excusing title, capacity, fraud or a specific indemnity.

**Push back:** Delete the “including matters discoverable from the data room or public records” qualifier. Replace with knowledge of *specific* seller knowledge persons doing reasonable enquiries — never assuming the buyer knew everything publicly.

### 6. Disclosure = deemed discovery, not fair disclosure
Schedule 7 frames the disclosure as “general reliance on the data room and public registers.” The Disclosure Letter [1.1]-[1.2] mirror this: broad electronic room + “publicly searchable corporate records,” “without limiting any specific disclosure below.”

We require *specific* fair disclosure — targeted claims, named facts, tailored representations. This package offers generic room dumps. A buyer who relied on a proper search can recover under standard principles; one who relied on this letter gets nothing.

**Push back:** Demand the disclosure Letter be rewritten as specific fair disclosures for each DD box, not a general blanket. Require each item to stand alone; delete the“without limiting any specific disclosure below” language.

### 7. Bluefen: consent treated as satisfied, no evidence of conditions met
DD-002 ~AUD 3.6M FY26 revenue (~30%) is a material customer. Playbook requires effective consent **before Completion** plus *evidence* that associated conditions are satisfied. Reasonable endeavours alone is insufficient for a material customer.

Disclosure letter admits: “As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.” The Seller still proposes treating consent as satisfied on delivery of a counterparty’s written consent — a red flag.

**Push back:** Make Bluefen consent a Condition Precedent with prior completion of the change-control conditions, evidenced by written consent + completion evidence, taken out of completion. Do not treat it as satisfied on delivery.

### 8. Riverlark: no repayment plan, no Release, no undertaking
~AUD 3.2M outstanding. Playbook: current payout, direct repayment from Completion funds, *effective security release*, and a post-completion Release requiring an irrevocable undertaking + Amelia Frost approval.

Nothing here addresses any of those. The Disclosure Letter admits the facility has not been repaid and no final discharge is included.

**Push back:** Require a current repayment schedule run off Completion funds. Secure an irrevocable undertaking from the Seller to repay by a date, and require formal security releases (not just “release following Completion”). If any release is post-completion, add the irrevocable undertaking and Amelia approval gate.

### 9. Employee bonuses: silently omitted from funds flow
DD-005 AUD 420,000 with triggered on-costs must appear as a specific line item or be seller-funded. The Seller’s completion fund flow does not itemise them. Silent exclusion is exactly the trap we warned against.

**Push back:** Insert the A
=== END ADVICE ===
